_comment_file: Every failure the core can hand the interface, keyed by the stable `code` on `IpcError` (crates/remoter-ipc/src/error.rs). The code is the join: the core sends a code, a sentence, an optional diagnostic and an ordered list of next actions, and this file supplies the sentence and the actions in the reader's language. A code with no entry here is not broken — the core's own English is rendered instead, which is what a failure newly added in Rust should look like until it is translated. Four rules for anyone editing this file. (1) `actions` is positional: the order is the order the core offered, and a label is used only when the entry has one at that position. (2) No sentence here may quote a password, a passphrase, a key or any other secret — a failure is the one moment an implementation is tempted to say what it was given. (3) The sentences carry no placeholders. The core fills its own sentence with the specifics (a path, a slot number, a byte offset) and those cannot be recovered from the finished string, so each sentence here is written to stay true without them; an English reader is shown the core's own sentence, specifics and all, and every other language is shown this one. (4) A message says what failed and what the reader can do about it. 'An error occurred' is never an acceptable translation of anything below.

unknown._comment_: Not a code the core sends: `asFailure` in apps/desktop/ui/src/lib/ipc.ts uses it when a rejection arrives with no shape at all — a panic inside a command, or a transport failure below Tauri. It is the last sentence in the application and should never be reached.

vault._comment_unlock-failed: SECURITY-CRITICAL. This sentence must not say which factor was wrong, and a translation must not add that either: before a key slot has unwrapped the master key, naming the password or the key file as the wrong one tells an attacker which half they have already guessed. See the module docs in crates/remoter-ipc/src/error.rs.
